## A score from one survey is an estimate

Most pages so far have reported a model's score as a single number. That number comes from
one survey: had other sites on the same coast been sampled, the cross-validated RMSE would
have come out higher or lower, and two models might have swapped places. Before a score is
reported, or used to choose between models, it is worth knowing how far it could move. This
page puts an interval on a cross-validated score, and shows that comparing two models needs
an interval of its own, much narrower than either model's.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

{{< include ../../_snippets/python-tabs-run.qmd >}}

## Resampling the sites gives a score its interval

[Dependent data](../06-assumptions-limitations/dependent-data.qmd#resampling-whole-groups-measures-the-effective-sample-size)
drew bootstrap samples of whole sites to see how far an estimate moves from one sample
to the next. A score can be treated the same way. Cross-validation has already given every
station an out-of-fold prediction, as on
[Cross-validation](cross-validation.qmd#out-of-fold-predictions-are-pooled-into-one-score).
A bootstrap sample draws the sites again, with replacement, keeps each drawn site's
stations with their predictions, and works out the RMSE on them. Repeated a thousand times,
this gives a thousand RMSEs. The middle 95% of them, from the 2.5th to the 97.5th
percentile, is a 95%
[confidence interval](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd) for the score.

Nothing is refitted, so a thousand samples take a second or two. The models are held fixed,
though: the interval shows how much the score depends on which sites were scored, not how
the models themselves would change if fitted to other sites. Refitting in every sample would
add that, at a thousand times the cost.

## Two models are compared in pairs

Two models scored on the same sites share most of what makes a score high or low. A site
with a few very large catches raises every model's RMSE, and a site of near-empty stations
lowers them all. So when the sites are drawn again, the two scores rise and fall together,
and their intervals can overlap widely even when one model is better in almost every
sample. A **paired comparison** works out the difference between the two scores within each
bootstrap sample, so that what they share cancels. The interval of that difference says how
sure the ranking is.

::: {.diagram}
![Two models scored on five resamples. Scored alone, each model's error moves widely from one resample to the next, and the two intervals overlap almost entirely. In pairs, the difference between the two errors is nearly the same in every resample, and its interval is short and clear of zero.](img/paired-comparison.svg){fig-alt="Two cards. Left, scored alone, the intervals overlap: five resamples, each with the error of model A, a blue dot, and of model B, an orange dot, joined by a short line. From one resample to the next both errors move together, between 3.4 and 5.3, and B is always a little lower. Below, model A's interval runs from 3.6 to 5.3 and model B's from 3.4 to 5.0, so the two overlap almost entirely. Right, in pairs, the difference is clear: the same five resamples give one green dot each, the error of B minus the error of A, between minus 0.4 and minus 0.2, all to the left of a dashed line at zero. Its interval is short and clear of zero. A note says a hard resample is hard for both models, so their errors rise and fall together; their difference cancels what they share, so it is far more certain than either error."}
:::

Pairing needs both models to have predicted the same stations from the same folds, which
is why every page in this section fits all its models on one set of folds.

## Worked example

The models are three of the four on
[Regression performance measures](regression-metrics.qmd):

- **Predicting the average**, with no skill.
- **Linear regression**, the simple baseline.
- **Random forest**.

They are cross-validated on the same ten folds of sites as on that page, so their
out-of-fold predictions and RMSEs are the same. A thousand bootstrap samples of the sites
then give each score its interval, and give each pair of models a paired difference.

### Preparing the data

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()

set.seed(61)
folds <- group_vfold_cv(survey, group = site_id, v = 10)

inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu",
            "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude")

with_inputs <- function(model) {
  recipe(reformulate(inputs, "abundance"), data = survey) |>
    step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    workflow(model)
}

forest <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |>
  set_mode("regression")

models <- list(
  "Predicting the average" = with_inputs(null_model(mode = "regression")),
  "Linear regression"      = with_inputs(linear_reg()),
  "Random forest"          = with_inputs(forest)
)

# every station's out-of-fold prediction from each model, in the survey's order
out_of_fold <- map(models, \(model) {
  fit_resamples(model, folds, metrics = metric_set(rmse),
                control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |>
    collect_predictions() |>
    arrange(.row) |>
    pull(.pred)
})

scored <- as_tibble(out_of_fold) |>
  mutate(site_id = survey$site_id, caught = survey$abundance)

rmse_by_model <- function(data) {
  map_dbl(set_names(names(models)), \(m) rmse_vec(data$caught, data[[m]]))
}

tibble(stations = nrow(survey), sites = n_distinct(survey$site_id))
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean

survey = load_coastal_survey_clean()
caught = survey["abundance"].to_numpy()

folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=61)

inputs = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu",
          "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude"]
categorical = ["substrate", "season"]
numeric = [c for c in inputs if c not in categorical]

def with_inputs(model):
    recipe = ColumnTransformer([
        ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric),
        ("nominal", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical),
    ])
    return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", model)])

# max_features="sqrt" draws a few inputs at each question, as ranger does.
forest = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt",
                               min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=1)

models = {
    "Predicting the average": DummyRegressor(),
    "Linear regression": LinearRegression(),
    "Random forest": forest,
}

# every station's out-of-fold prediction from each model, in the survey's order
out_of_fold = {name: cross_val_predict(with_inputs(model), survey[inputs], caught,
                                       cv=folds, groups=survey["site_id"])
               for name, model in models.items()}

def rmse_by_model(rows):
    return {name: root_mean_squared_error(caught[rows], predicted[rows])
            for name, predicted in out_of_fold.items()}

pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(survey)], "sites": [survey["site_id"].nunique()]})
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: helpers
#| include: false
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
pct <- function(x) scales::percent(x, accuracy = 1)
n_sites <- n_distinct(survey$site_id)
```

The survey's `r nrow(survey)` stations come from `r n_sites` sites, so each bootstrap
sample draws `r n_sites` sites with replacement, some of them twice or more and others not
at all.

### Each model's interval is wider than the gaps between the models

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: intervals
set.seed(62)
site_samples <- group_bootstraps(scored, group = site_id, times = 1000)

# one row per bootstrap sample, one column per model
scores <- map(site_samples$splits, \(s) as_tibble_row(rmse_by_model(analysis(s)))) |>
  list_rbind()

intervals <- tibble(
  model = names(models),
  RMSE  = rmse_by_model(scored),
  lower = map_dbl(scores, \(x) quantile(x, 0.025)),
  upper = map_dbl(scores, \(x) quantile(x, 0.975))
) |>
  mutate(width = upper - lower)

intervals |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

## Python

```{python}
sites = survey["site_id"].to_numpy()
site_rows = [np.flatnonzero(sites == s) for s in np.unique(sites)]

# draw the sites again, with replacement, and score every model on their stations
rng = np.random.default_rng(62)
samples = []
for sample in range(1000):
    drawn = rng.integers(len(site_rows), size=len(site_rows))
    rows = np.concatenate([site_rows[i] for i in drawn])
    samples.append(rmse_by_model(rows))
scores = pd.DataFrame(samples)

intervals = pd.DataFrame({
    "model": list(models),
    "RMSE": list(rmse_by_model(np.arange(len(survey))).values()),
    "lower": scores.quantile(0.025).to_numpy(),
    "upper": scores.quantile(0.975).to_numpy(),
})
intervals["width"] = intervals["upper"] - intervals["lower"]

intervals.round(3)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: interval-numbers
#| include: false
interval_of <- function(m) {
  row <- filter(intervals, model == m)
  glue::glue("{f2(row$RMSE)} ({f2(row$lower)} to {f2(row$upper)})")
}
score_of <- function(m) intervals$RMSE[intervals$model == m]
gap_average <- score_of("Predicting the average") - score_of("Random forest")
gap_linear <- score_of("Linear regression") - score_of("Random forest")
```

Each RMSE is shown with its 95% interval: predicting the average
`r interval_of("Predicting the average")`, linear regression
`r interval_of("Linear regression")` and the random forest
`r interval_of("Random forest")`. The intervals are `r f2(min(intervals$width))` to
`r f2(max(intervals$width))` wide, more than twice the forest's lead of `r f2(gap_average)`
over predicting the average, and many times its lead of `r f2(gap_linear)` over linear
regression. Read alone, the three intervals overlap, and cannot say which model is better:
not even whether either model beats predicting the average.

### Pairing separates the forest from the average but not from linear regression

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: paired
full <- rmse_by_model(scored)

differences <- map(c("Predicting the average", "Linear regression"), \(other) {
  in_each_sample <- scores$`Random forest` - scores[[other]]
  tibble(`forest minus` = other,
         difference = full[["Random forest"]] - full[[other]],
         lower = quantile(in_each_sample, 0.025),
         upper = quantile(in_each_sample, 0.975),
         `samples with the forest lower` = mean(in_each_sample < 0))
}) |>
  list_rbind()

differences |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

## Python

```{python}
full = rmse_by_model(np.arange(len(survey)))

table_rows = []
for other in ["Predicting the average", "Linear regression"]:
    in_each_sample = scores["Random forest"] - scores[other]
    table_rows.append({"forest minus": other,
                       "difference": full["Random forest"] - full[other],
                       "lower": in_each_sample.quantile(0.025),
                       "upper": in_each_sample.quantile(0.975),
                       "samples with the forest lower": (in_each_sample < 0).mean()})
differences = pd.DataFrame(table_rows)

differences.round(3)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: paired-numbers
#| include: false
paired_of <- function(m) filter(differences, `forest minus` == m)
vs_average <- paired_of("Predicting the average")
vs_linear <- paired_of("Linear regression")
signed <- function(x) sub("^-", "−", f2(x))
paired_width <- vs_linear$upper - vs_linear$lower
together <- cor(scores$`Random forest`, scores$`Linear regression`)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-pairs
#| fig-cap: !expr glue::glue("The forest's RMSE against another model's in each of the 1,000 bootstrap samples of sites. Points below the dashed diagonal are samples in which the forest scored better. Against predicting the average, it did in {pct(vs_average[[5]])} of samples. Against linear regression the points hug the diagonal, as the two scores rise and fall together, and the forest did better in {pct(vs_linear[[5]])}.")
#| fig-alt: !expr glue::glue("Two square scatter plots side by side, each with a dashed diagonal line. Each has 1,000 points, one per bootstrap sample, with the forest's RMSE on the vertical axis. In the left panel the horizontal axis is the RMSE of predicting the average; the points form a long cloud running from about {f2(min(scores[[1]]))} to {f2(max(scores[[1]]))} along it, almost all of them below the diagonal. In the right panel the horizontal axis is the RMSE of linear regression; the points form a long, narrow band lying along the diagonal, most of them just below it and some just above.")
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.6
paired_scores <- scores |>
  pivot_longer(c(`Predicting the average`, `Linear regression`),
               names_to = "other", values_to = "other_rmse") |>
  mutate(other = str_to_lower(other),
         other = fct_inorder(paste("Against", other)),
         better = if_else(`Random forest` < other_rmse,
                          "Forest lower", "Forest higher"))

limits <- range(c(scores$`Random forest`, paired_scores$other_rmse))

ggplot(paired_scores, aes(other_rmse, `Random forest`, colour = better)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey50", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 0.9, alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~other) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Forest lower" = ml_palette[["blue"]],
                                 "Forest higher" = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]),
                      breaks = c("Forest lower", "Forest higher")) +
  coord_equal(xlim = limits, ylim = limits) +
  labs(x = "RMSE of the other model (individuals)",
       y = "RMSE of the forest (individuals)", colour = NULL) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

:::

Against predicting the average, the forest's RMSE is lower by `r f2(-vs_average$difference)`,
with a paired 95% interval from `r signed(vs_average$lower)` to `r signed(vs_average$upper)`.
The interval lies clear of zero, and the forest scored better in
`r pct(vs_average[[5]])` of the samples, although the two models' own intervals overlap.

Against linear regression the paired interval runs from `r signed(vs_linear$lower)` to
`r signed(vs_linear$upper)`. At `r f2(paired_width)` wide, against
`r f2(min(intervals$width))` for the narrowest of the models' own intervals, it is far
sharper, because the two scores move almost in step (their correlation across the samples
is `r f2(together)`). It still covers zero. The forest
did better in `r pct(vs_linear[[5]])` of the samples, so the order on
[Regression performance measures](regression-metrics.qmd) is not stable: on this survey,
RMSE cannot tell the forest from linear regression.

## Overlapping intervals do not show that two models are alike

Report each score with its interval and the number of sites behind it. Compare two models by
their paired difference, never by whether their own intervals overlap: here every interval
overlapped the others, and the forest still beat predicting the average in nearly every
sample. A lead that holds in `r pct(vs_linear[[5]])` of samples is not yet a result. For a method with
random choices in the fit, a difference must also be larger than the spread from one run to
the next, which
[Reproducibility and transparent reporting](../10-interpretation/reproducibility.qmd)
measures by changing the seed. The Python tab shows why: its forest, grown from other
random draws, beats linear regression in nearly every sample.

## Key points

::: {.key-points}
- A cross-validated score comes from one survey, and would move if other sites had been
  sampled. Here each model's 95% interval was `r f2(min(intervals$width))` to
  `r f2(max(intervals$width))` wide.
- A bootstrap of the sites over the pooled out-of-fold predictions gives that interval
  without refitting. It holds the fitted models fixed.
- Two models are compared by a **paired comparison**: the difference in score within each
  bootstrap sample, on the same folds. What the two share cancels, so the paired interval
  is much narrower than either model's own.
- The forest beat predicting the average in `r pct(vs_average[[5]])` of samples, although
  their own intervals overlapped. It beat linear regression in only
  `r pct(vs_linear[[5]])`, and the paired interval covered zero.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Score the models with the MAE (`mae_vec()`) instead of the RMSE. Can the forest and
   linear regression be told apart now?
2. Draw single stations instead of whole sites (`bootstraps()` in place of
   `group_bootstraps()`). How much narrower do the intervals become, and why are they
   too narrow?
